name: Resveratrol
lead: Resveratrol (3,5,4'-trihydroxy-trans-stilbene) is a polyphenol of the stilbenoid class produced by plants such as grapes, blueberries, raspberries, mulberries and peanuts in response to injury or pathogens [1]. Most US supplements are derived from the root of Japanese knotweed [1]. It is sold as an oral supplement and is an ingredient in some skincare products, and it became widely known through laboratory reports that it activates sirtuins and extends lifespan in some organisms [2][3].

It is promoted for longevity, skin ageing, metabolic health and cardiovascular protection. Wikipedia states there is no high-quality evidence that it improves human lifespan or has a substantial effect on any human disease [1]. Reviews of its pharmacokinetics describe about 75% oral absorption but extensive intestinal and hepatic metabolism, leaving oral bioavailability of the free compound below 1% [4][5].
In bodybuilding and testosterone-therapy forums, resveratrol is also discussed as a natural aromatase inhibitor and anti-inflammatory supplement, claims that are mainly anecdotal [6][7][8].

paras: Resveratrol exists as cis and trans isomers, with trans the form usually studied and sold; the trans form can convert to cis under ultraviolet light [1]. In plants it is made by stilbene synthase from precursors derived from phenylalanine [1]. Content in food varies widely: red wine averages under 2 mg per litre of trans-resveratrol, with a reported range from undetectable to about 14 mg per litre, and peanuts and mulberries also contain it [1]. Wikipedia notes that the low food levels make dietary intake much smaller than the amounts used in supplement studies [1].

Wikipedia dates the first mention to a 1939 Japanese article by Michio Takaoka, who isolated it from Veratrum album, and to 1963 for its isolation from Japanese knotweed roots [1]. A 1997 Science paper reported cancer chemopreventive activity of resveratrol from grapes in laboratory assays [9]. In 2003 a Nature paper reported that small-molecule sirtuin activators, including resveratrol, extended yeast lifespan, and a 2006 Nature paper reported improved health and survival in mice on a high-calorie diet [2][3]. Related 2006 work in Cell reported effects on mitochondrial function through SIRT1 and PGC-1 alpha [10].

In 2004 Harvard professor David Sinclair co-founded Sirtris Pharmaceuticals, whose first product was a resveratrol formulation. GlaxoSmithKline bought Sirtris in 2008 for 720 million dollars and shut it down in 2013 without a successful drug, according to Wikipedia [1]. A phase 1 trial of the formulation SRT501 in colorectal cancer with liver metastases and a phase 2 trial in multiple myeloma were registered, with the latter terminated [11][12].

Resveratrol is used in anti-ageing skincare for its antioxidant properties. A systematic review of its effects on wound healing, scarring and ageing of skin summarised the preclinical and clinical literature, and Wikipedia states there is no significant evidence that it affects ageing skin in humans [13][1]. A review of cosmeceuticals in photoaging also compares botanicals including polyphenols with other topical agents [14].
In physique communities it is also used for perceived hormonal effects such as lowering estrogen, discussed below.

Resveratrol has been tested in type 2 diabetes, ulcerative colitis, Alzheimer's disease, bone health in postmenopausal women, Friedreich ataxia, endothelial function and cancer, mostly in small trials [15][16][17][18][19][20][21][22]. It has no approved drug indication.

Proposed mechanisms include activation of SIRT1 and AMPK, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity and effects on NF-kappa B signalling [23][24]. Wikipedia reports that resveratrol has been identified as a pan-assay interference compound, giving positive results in many laboratory assays, and that it is classed as a phytoestrogen with diverse hormonal effects; many reported molecular targets have not been confirmed as responsible for effects in organisms [1]. The sirtuin activation hypothesis has been the subject of scientific debate, and a 2008 paper discussed how animal doses are translated to human doses [25][1].

Oral absorption in humans is high but conjugation to glucuronides and sulfates in the intestine and liver leaves bioavailability of the parent compound under 1%, and dose escalation or repeated dosing does not appear to change this substantially [4][5]. The half-life of the parent is minutes, while conjugated metabolites persist for hours [1].

Wikipedia's summary of the human literature states that resveratrol does not affect cardiovascular biomarkers, has little evidence for diabetes or metabolic syndrome, and has insufficient evidence for lifespan or cancer effects, with mixed evidence for cognition [1]. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of resveratrol in type 2 diabetes is available [26].

A randomised, placebo-controlled trial of 110 patients with type 2 diabetes on oral hypoglycaemic drugs examined glucose homeostasis, inflammation, oxidative stress and microRNA expression [15]. A multicentre trial in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis compared Mediterranean diet alone, with curcumin, and with resveratrol over 8 weeks [16]. A phase II trial in Alzheimer's disease reported effects on neuroinflammation and adaptive immunity [17]. A randomised trial in postmenopausal women reported improved bone mineral density with regular resveratrol supplementation [18], and another reported that equol with resveratrol improved bone turnover markers [27].

Registered trials include studies in healthy adults for inflammation and oxidative status, type 2 diabetes with inflammation, Friedreich ataxia, Gulf War illness and eye-tissue pharmacokinetics [28][29][19][30][31]. No published randomised trial has established a visible anti-ageing effect on skin from oral resveratrol.

Wikipedia reports that few human adverse-effect studies exist, all preliminary, with nausea, stomach pain, flatulence and diarrhoea mainly at daily doses of 1,000 mg or more over weeks; in a review of 136 patients receiving more than 500 mg for a month, diarrhoea was the most frequent complaint [1]. Because it acts as a phytoestrogen, possible endocrine effects have been raised [1]. Reviews of herbal and supplement safety also discuss potential interactions with anticoagulant drugs and drugs metabolised by CYP enzymes [32]. A forum user on antiplatelet therapy reported bleeding gums after adding resveratrol and bromelain [8].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and physique communities
paras: T Nation articles and threads describe resveratrol as a polyphenol that reduces insulin resistance and inflammation, counters endocrine disruptors, and acts as an aromatase inhibitor, and some users suggest it as a step alongside or instead of prescription anastrozole during testosterone therapy [6][33][7][34][8]. Other posts recommend it to slow glycation and ageing or list it with curcumin for inflammation [35][36]. Users sometimes ask what dose works, and replies vary [37].

lore.intro: In training forums resveratrol is discussed as an anti-ageing polyphenol and as a natural aromatase inhibitor for managing estradiol [6][7][8].

claims.claim: Resveratrol is a powerful natural aromatase inhibitor that lowers estrogen
claims.believers: T Nation authors and posters say it prevents testosterone converting to estrogen and some use it alongside or in place of anastrozole [7][34][8].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes resveratrol as a phytoestrogen with diverse hormonal effects, and none of the clinical studies reviewed establishes a clinically meaningful aromatase-inhibiting effect in men.

claims.claim: Resveratrol slows ageing and extends lifespan
claims.believers: Posters cite grape-skin polyphenol studies and mouse results of improved fitness and mitochondrial function [38][35].
claims.experts: It extended lifespan in some model organisms and improved survival in mice on high-calorie diets, but there is insufficient evidence for lifespan effects in humans [3][1].

claims.claim: It protects against heart disease and insulin resistance
claims.believers: A T Nation list of top supplements says it can protect from insulin resistance and heart disease [6].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports meta-analyses finding little or no effect on cardiovascular biomarkers and little evidence for diabetes, with small effects in subgroups [1].

claims.claim: It counters endocrine-disrupting chemicals and inflammation
claims.believers: T Nation articles say it combats phthalate-related endocrine disruption and inhibits NF-kB and pro-inflammatory cytokines [33][36].
claims.experts: Laboratory studies show effects on NF-kB signalling, while clinical evidence for these claims in healthy people is limited [24][1].
